title: perf-incident-postmortem-customer-escalation-2026-03
content:
Summary:

On 2026-03-14 we received a customer escalation (JIRA-1234) reporting intermittent SLO misses for their low-latency chat endpoint. The customer measured p95 latency spikes exceeding the 200ms SLO, with observed p95 up to ~520ms during incidents. The incident affected a single Dedicated cluster serving a high-throughput customer (burst traffic pattern). This doc summarizes timeline, impact, root cause analysis, profiling results, hotfix and validation, and follow-up actions.

Impact:
- Duration: 2026-03-14 09:22 UTC -> 2026-03-14 13:05 UTC (partial degradation; mitigations applied at 11:30, hotfix rolled 13:00)
- Scope: One Dedicated cluster (eu-west-1), affecting ~2% of total customer requests for the day but the customer was on an aggressive latency SLO contract.
- Symptoms: p95 latency spikes from baseline ~120ms to peaks ~520ms; increased queue length and backpressure; no widespread 5xx errors but elevated client timeouts reported.
- Customer impact: degraded UX for chat (delays), raised support escalations and financial SLA query.

Initial detection & timeline:
- 2026-03-14 09:15 UTC: Internal alerting triggered for p95>300ms on the eu-west-1 serving cluster (automated SLO monitor).
- 09:22 UTC: Support ticket opened; CS informed eng on-call.
- 09:35 UTC: On-call (Ava Martinez) began triage; confirmed p95 and queue growth.
- 09:52 UTC: Initial mitigation - increased max_inflight_requests on batcher as temporary measure; minor improvement but spikes persisted.
- 10:15 UTC: Profiling session started on a canary node using perf counters, nvprof traces, and custom sampling of request lifecycle (ingest->batch->kv-read->inference->serialize).
- 11:30 UTC: Applied targeted traffic routing: diverted a subset of customer traffic to alternative model variant with slightly lower memory footprint to relieve pressure. Immediate p95 improvement to ~220ms but still above SLO.
- 12:10 UTC: PR with hotfix prepared (https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/789).
- 13:00 UTC: Hotfix deployed to cluster (rolling restart per node), validation in staging complete.
- 13:05 UTC: Metrics returned to acceptable levels (p95 ~180ms). Customer notified; post-incident review started.

Root cause analysis (high level):
Our investigation shows a combination of factors: 1) a KV-cache eviction edge case that caused repeated CPU->GPU host-device synchronous copies for certain request shapes, 2) increased lock contention in the request batching queue under bursty traffic, and 3) degraded GPU occupancy because several batches fell back to a slower execution path (unfused kernels) when sequence-length distribution skewed unexpectedly. These together produced higher tail latency during bursts.

Evidence and profiling findings:
- Request-level traces: correlation between high p95 windows and requests that hit a KV-cache miss path. When misses occurred, the code path performed a host-side allocation and memcpy for each KV chunk before dispatching CUDA kernels. Sampling traces show the memcpy accounted for ~35% of per-request latency during spikes.
- nvprof / Nsight logs: increased PCIe transfer time during incidents (avg host->device transfer increased 4x vs baseline for affected requests). GPU kernel execution times were stable for normal batches but dropped in parallelism when batch composition included a high fraction of long-sequence requests.
- CPU metrics: CPU usage increased on the serving nodes (user time) and several worker threads stalled waiting on a mutex for the batcher queue. Contention measured using perf showed mutex hold time increased 6x during bursts.
- Batcher metrics: batch formation latency increased (time to fill batch) leading to wider variance in batch sizes; observed many small batches (<4 requests) which hurt GPU throughput and increased latency variance.
- Experiments: Replaying traces on staging with instrumentation reproduced the p95 spikes when forcing KV-cache misses + bursty traffic. Replaying with hotfixes disabled matched production spike patterns.

Root cause(s) (concrete):
1) KV-cache miss-fast-path performed repeated synchronous host->device memcpys per KV-chunk instead of aggregating and doing a single batched transfer; this was introduced as a micro-optimization in an earlier change (PR committed in 2026-02) and didn't trigger under the previous workload mix.
2) Batcher queue lock had a hot path where the lock was held while performing a small amount of bookkeeping; under bursty arrivals this serialized many producers and increased batch formation latency.
3) Sequence-length skew caused fallback to unfused kernels for a subset of model shims, reducing GPU occupancy and making the system more sensitive to CPU-side transfer overheads.

Immediate mitigations applied:
- Traffic routing to alternative model variant (11:30 UTC) to reduce long-sequence requests hitting the affected code path.
- Temporary increase to max_inflight_requests and lowered batch latency threshold to favor slightly larger batches (09:52 and 10:00 UTC) — helped throughput but increased p99 for some requests; reverted after hotfix.
- Hotfix PR #789 (12:10 UTC):
  - Aggregate KV-chunk copies into a single contiguous host buffer per request group and use a single async host->device copy per group.
  - Reduce lock hold duration in batcher by moving bookkeeping outside the critical section and using a per-producer staging queue to reduce contention.
  - Add a fallback threshold that avoids unfused kernel fallback for small batches when GPU occupancy would be low.

Hotfix validation and benchmarks:
Validation plan executed in staging before rollout:
- Unit and integration tests: run full CI (passed).
- Microbenchmarks: compared baseline (pre-hotfix) vs hotfix under two synthetic workloads: (A) steady throughput with uniform seq lengths and (B) bursty traffic with skewed long-sequence fraction.
  - Workload A: p95 baseline 115ms -> hotfix 110ms (no regression). Throughput unchanged.
  - Workload B (replay of customer trace): p95 baseline 480ms -> hotfix 175ms. p99 baseline 720ms -> hotfix 260ms. GPU utilization increased 12 percentage points; PCIe transfer time reduced by ~70% for affected requests.
- End-to-end load test with canary ramp: 30-minute soak at 1.2x customer peak with real request shapes. Observed stable p95 ~180ms, queue length stable, no CPU thread contention spikes.
- Canary rollout: rolled hotfix to 10% of nodes for 20 minutes, monitor, then full cluster rollout (rolling restarts). Observed metrics matched staging.

Post-deploy metrics (production):
- p95 latency returned to ~180ms (below 200ms SLO) within 5 minutes of completion.
- p99 reduced to ~240ms, down from >700ms.
- No increase in 5xx rates.
- Customer confirmed improved UX and accepted incident summary.

Communication and customer handling:
- 2026-03-14 14:00 UTC: Sent initial technical summary and mitigation steps to customer.
- 2026-03-15: Follow-up call with customer to review root cause and validated fixes; customer requested SLA credit claim (CS queued with finance).

Action items / next steps (owners):
- eng-serving-runtime: Backport hotfix to all supported branches and include in private deployment images (owner: Rahul Mehta, due 2026-03-21).
- eng-serving-runtime: Add automated reproducer (fuzzing harness) for KV-cache miss + bursty traffic patterns into perf-test suite (owner: Sophie Chen, due 2026-04-01).
- eng-serving-runtime: Add observability dashboards for KV-cache miss rate, aggregated PCIe transfer latency per request, and per-batcher lock contention metrics (owner: Diego Alvarez, due 2026-03-22).
- product & support: Update customer-facing runbook and incident FAQ for SLO miss escalation and mitigation steps (owner: CS team, due 2026-03-25).
- reliability: Review batching defaults and consider adaptive batcher config that weights recent seq-length distribution (owner: SRE, due 2026-04-05).

Postmortem notes and learnings:
- Small micro-optimizations that look safe under average load can create large tail regressions under skewed workloads; need stronger perf regression harnesses that include tail-case inputs.
- Observability gaps: we did not have a single metric that clearly surfaced KV-cache miss as a first-order signal; adding derived metrics would speed triage.
- Batcher contention is an easy-to-introduce source of tail latency; guardrails (mutex hold-time alerts) should be part of default dashboards.
